title: FIFE_SOIL_REL_112
abstract: This data product was developed based on the hypothesis that various ground truth observations of soil moisture could be integrated to estimate uniform soil moisture contours over a large area, such as the FIFE area. The next phase involved using spatial statistical methods to interpolate these contours, resulting in average soil moisture values at the nodes of a uniform grid. Each grid node value represents the average soil moisture over a 0.5 km x 0.5 km area centered at the node location. The correlation area method (CAM) was utilized to combine in situ measurements with airborne gamma remote sensing estimates to obtain areal averages of soil moisture. Additionally, a model incorporating information on biomass and the spatial distribution of vegetation was used to estimate soil moisture from PBMR (Push Broom Microwave Radiometer) measurements. Another simpler method, relying solely on ground soil moisture data, was also employed to compute soil moisture from PBMR measurements. All collected soil moisture data from aircraft platforms and ground measurements were entered into the ARC/INFO GIS, including the UTM coordinates of each observation. An analysis of all available and usable soil moisture measurements was conducted to produce isolines of soil moisture.

The forest soils are sandy, hydromorphic podzols with dark organic matter in the top 30 cm, and a distinct litter layer of organic matter that can exceed 10 cm in thickness.

title: SCAN
abstract: The National Water and Climate Center (NWCC), based in Portland, Oregon, supports the Snow Survey and Water Supply Forecasting (SSWSF) Program and the Soil Climate Analysis Network (SCAN) Program. As part of the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation Service, the NWCC is tasked with producing and disseminating accurate and reliable water supply forecasts and other climatic data to a diverse range of users. All data collected by the NWCC are quality-controlled and stored in a comprehensive database called the Water and Climate Information System (WCIS). This database includes data from automated SNOTEL and manual snow data collection processes, as well as precipitation, streamflow, and reservoir data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (BOR), the Applied Climate Information System (ACIS), the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), various water districts, and other entities. In 1991, the NWCC launched a pilot project for the Soil Climate Analysis Network (SCAN), which monitors and reports soil moisture, soil temperature, and other climate data at over 200 sites across the U.S. More recently, the Tribal Soil Climate Analysis Network (Tribal SCAN) was developed to serve Tribal lands throughout the country. Data from SCAN and Tribal SCAN are also integrated into the WCIS.

title: SNOTEL
abstract: SNOTEL is an automated, remote, telemetered, large-scale, long-term, and low-latency mountain snowpack and weather monitoring network. Operated by the United States Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), it consists of 890 sites across the western U.S. and Alaska (Perkins et al., 2009; Schaefer & Paetzold, 2000; Strobel et al., 2009). Standard SNOTEL stations measure several critical hydrometeorological variables, including Snow Water Equivalent (SWE), snow depth, precipitation, and air temperature. The SNOTEL network has been enhanced by the relatively new SNOtel LITE (SNOLITE) network, which now includes over 40 automated stations that measure at least two of the four core SNOTEL parameters. Additionally, enhanced SNOTEL sites are equipped with extra sensors to address specific local resource management concerns, measuring soil moisture, relative humidity, solar radiation, wind speed/direction, or other important metrics. The SNOTEL network began in the late 1950s to early 1960s to collect and transmit information from existing snowpack measurement locations 1 day. Many SNOTEL sites replaced manual snow courses. Initially, transmitters at these sites used roll recorders to report SWE and employed radio/repeater arrays to telemeter data to state Data Collection Offices (DCOs). With the advent of new radio technologies during the Cold War, the network transitioned to using innovative Meteorburst communications to relay data from remote weather stations to centralized databases.

title: SOILSCAPE
abstract: The SoilSCAPE (Soil moisture Sensing Controller and oPtimal Estimator) project aims to address the need for soil moisture information by providing local scale estimates of soil moisture with high temporal resolution (<1 hour) and validation data to evaluate the accuracy of soil moisture estimates from remote sensing data at regional (airborne) and national (spaceborne) scales. To achieve these goals, wireless sensor networks that record soil moisture are being installed at various sites. The optimal placement of nodes and scheduling is determined through modeling as part of the project's Control System element. Each sensor measures soil moisture at a specific point. To scale these estimates up to a regional level, hydrological models incorporate additional data (such as soil type, topography, and precipitation) to produce local scale estimates of soil moisture. Soil moisture measurements are being used as validation data for two NASA missions: the Airborne Microwave Observation of Subcanopy and Subsurface Mission (AirMOSS), currently flying, and the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission, planned for launch in 2014. Both missions estimate soil moisture using microwave technology.

title: SoilSCAPE_V2_2049
abstract: This dataset comprises in-situ soil moisture pro and soil temperature data collected at 30-minute intervals across various SoilSCAPE (Soil moisture Sensing Controller and oPtimal Estimator) project sites since 2021, spanning locations in the United States and New Zealand. Employing wireless sensor technology, the SoilSCAPE network facilitates the acquisition of high temporal resolution soil moisture and temperature data, a capability in operation since 2011. Since 2021, SoilSCAPE has undergone upgrades, including the revitalization of two previously active sites in Arizona and the addition of several new sites across the United States and New Zealand. These new sites predominantly employ the METER Teros-12 soil moisture sensor. At its peak, the expanded network comprised 57 wireless sensor installations (nodes), with each site hosting between 6 to 8 nodes. Within each SoilSCAPE site, multiple wireless end-devices (EDs) are present, with each ED accommodating up to five soil moisture probes, typically installed at depth of 5, 10, 20, and 30 centimeters below the surface. In Arizona sites, soil moisture probes are installed at depth of up to 75 centimeters below the surface. Sensor placement may be constrained by soil conditions, such as hard soil or rocks. This dataset facilitates the estimation of local-scale soil moisture at high temporal resolution and serves as a means for validating remote sensing estimates of soil moisture at regional and national scales, including missions like NASA's Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) and Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP). The data are provided in NetCDF format, comprising a total of 43 s.

title: UGA
abstract: The Georgia Automated Environmental Monitoring Network was established in 1991 by the College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences of the University of Georgia. The objective of the AEMN is to collect reliable weather information for agricultural and environmental applications. Each station monitors air temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, solar radiation, wind speed, wind direction, soil temperature at 2, 4, and 8-inch depth, atmospheric pressure, and soil moisture every 1 second. Data are summarized at 15-minute intervals and at midnight a 1 day summary is calculated. A microcomputer at the Georgia Experiment Station initiates telephone calls to each station periodically and downloads the recorded data. The data are processed immediately and disseminated via the world wide web (www.weather.uga.edu)

title: USCRN
abstract: The U.S. Climate Reference Network (USCRN) is a systematic and sustained network of climate monitoring stations located across the conterminous U.S., Alaska, and Hawaii. These stations are equipped with high-quality instruments to measure temperature, precipitation, wind speed, soil conditions, and more. Detailed information on what is measured and the instruments used at USCRN stations is available. The vision of the USCRN program is to provide a continuous series of climate observations to monitor trends in the nation's climate and support climate-impact research. USCRN stations are managed and maintained by the Atmospheric Turbulence and Diffusion Division of the Air Resources Laboratory, part of the NOAA Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research. title: ARM
abstract: The ARM Mobile Facility (AMF) was deployed to Point Reyes National Seashore, California, to study marine stratus clouds, which are crucial yet understudied components of Earth's climate system. These clouds, sensitive to human-induced aerosols, have two stable states influenced by cloud condensation nuclei (CCN). Researchers aimed to explore the relationships among cloud structure, aerosols, microphysics, drizzle, and radiation, and to understand aerosols' impact on solar radiation absorption discrepancies between measurements and models. Detailed observations using radar, aircraft, and advanced radiation measurement tools were conducted, building on summer 2005 experiments supported by the Office of Naval Research and other agencies. The research involved sophisticated radar and aircraft measurements to improve the understanding of solar radiation absorption by these clouds.

title: FMI
abstract: The Arctic Space Centre of the Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI-ARC) is located in Sodankylä, Finnish Lapland. This region, part of the boreal forest zone due to the Gulf Stream's warming effect, is also classified as an Arctic site concerning stratospheric meteorology. Its high-latitude position is ideal for receiving data from polar orbiting satellites. The center hosts programs focused on upper-air chemistry and physics, snow and soil hydrology, carbon fluxes, biosphere-atmosphere interaction, and intelligent traffic. It specializes in the calibration and validation of Earth Observation (EO) satellite data, as well as model and algorithm development.
